diagnostic_evidence.quote: It is well established that the DN map uniquely determines an isotropic, essentially bounded conductivity. Consequently, the forward operator  $A: f\mapsto\Lambda_f$ is injective at $f^\dagger$ \cite{AstalaPaivarinta2006}.
It is worth noting that, although a single measurement pair is sufficient for the current model problem, employing multiple sets of boundary measurements

issues.failure_explanation: The injectivity cited (Astala-Paivarinta) concerns the full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map f -> Lambda_f (all boundary voltage/current pairs). The numerical scheme, however, solves the equation with the single-measurement operator f -> Lambda_f h_1, which maps the infinite-dimensional conductivity class to one boundary function; such a map is underdetermined and not injective in general, and no uniqueness result for it is given or cited. Theorems main and main2 (whose hypothesis is a continuous injective operator) therefore do not apply to the example as implemented, and the assertion that 'a single measurement pair is sufficient for the current model problem' is made without any support. The properties verified in the example (injectivity and Lipschitz estimates) concern a different operator than the one actually used in the algorithm.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either use the full DN map (or justify uniqueness of the single-measurement map on a restricted, e.g. finite-dimensional, conductivity class), or state explicitly that Example 3 is an empirical illustration lying outside the proved framework.
issues.overall_effect: The convergence/regularization guarantees of Theorems 1-2 invoked for the EIT experiment do not cover the numerical scheme as set up; Example 3, the paper's only 2D PDE example, loses its claimed theoretical backing.
issues.title: Example Ex3's implemented forward operator is a single-measurement DN map, for which the injectivity required by Theorems 1-2 is not available
issues.why_classification: The formal theory is unaffected, but the example as implemented has no theoretical guarantee; restoring coverage requires changing the experiment or restricting the unknown class - neither present in the source - which is more than a routine local repair.
